checks: Equivalence to intrinsic Hausdorff measure on each nonempty compact convex set gives positive mass to every neighborhood of each face point, including the singleton case. Thus the equal-radius hypothesis applies for every fixed x and every y in the other face at every positive radius.

The power-mean estimate supplies the factor 2^(-r). The inverse image of the radius-epsilon ball at T_x(y) is the radius-2epsilon ball at y, so the endpoint ball-mass ratio tends to 2^(-m_B) at points of finite positive intrinsic density. A zero-dimensional face has ratio one. Euclidean Radon-relative differentiation gives the derivative of the part of the middle measure absolutely continuous with respect to the pushforward. The lower bound on that derivative gives domination as measures, including any additional singular part of the middle measure.

The pushforward is nonzero and carried by an affine space of dimension m_B. If m_K were greater than m_B, that space would be intrinsically null for the middle face. Symmetry gives the bound with m_A. The linear span of midpoint-set differences is exactly the sum of endpoint directions, as follows by holding either endpoint fixed, so inclusion forces equality of all dimensions and directions. The common dimension and inclusion then identify the middle affine plane with the averaged endpoint affine planes.

Open ball mass is Borel in the center by integration of a Borel indicator. For each positive real radius, normalized ball mass is approximated by normalized masses at increasing rational radii below it. This gives the same upper and lower limits over all or rational radii, so the full endpoint sets and middle upper-density representative are Borel. The usual intrinsic Lebesgue differentiation theorem applies on the full affine planes using zero-extended densities.

At every pair of good endpoints, the equal-radius masses are positive and converge after normalization to the respective endpoint densities. Homogeneity and continuity yield the power-mean lower bound on the middle upper limit. Arithmetic-geometric mean gives P_r(s,t) at least sqrt(st), and its application to s^(-1/m), t^(-1/m) followed by raising to the negative power -m gives sqrt(st) at least the reciprocal-power bound.
